Babine

Also find this entry through: Lake Babine Nation (profile focus)

Babine histories connect lake and river communities, salmon fisheries, hereditary leadership, and relationships across north-central British Columbia. This introduction centers Lake Babine Nation’s own publications, alongside collaborative scholarship and public records. Its reading collection follows historical trade and colonial interference through language learning, community planning, stewardship, and work toward self-government.

Names & relationshipsThis profile centers Lake Babine Nation and its communities. Language labels such as Babine, Nedut’en, and Babine–Witsuwit’en require context; linguistic relationships do not make Lake Babine, Wet’suwet’en, or Dakelh governments interchangeable. The historical Barricade Treaty and the 2020 Foundation Agreement are different instruments.
An expanded introduction, with sources reviewed.This profile develops several themes through identified sources. Citations connect each section to its evidence; remaining gaps appear below. It has not been reviewed or endorsed by the community.
01

A nation of connected communities

Lake Babine Nation’s community plan organizes its discussion around Tachet, Fort Babine or Wit’at, Old Fort, Pinkut Lake/Donald’s Landing, and Woyenne, alongside members living away from home. This is a network of communities with shared and distinct priorities, rather than one village whose location captures the entire homeland. The treaty office’s public account places the traditional territory around Babine Lake and describes four clans and hereditary leaders with responsibilities toward land. Its institutional and treaty-stage descriptions are older material, however, and should not be taken as a current administrative directory.

Read the sources [1] Lake Babine Nation Treaty Office [2] Lake Babine Nation

02

Balhats and the study of law

The balhats, or feast system, belongs within an account of law, leadership, and responsibilities. In Cis dideen kat—When the Plumes Rise, Jo-Anne Fiske and Betty Patrick frame their study as a descriptive account of Lake Babine customary law and changing relations with the Canadian state. Their publicly available introductory chapter explains that research began in 1993 and that historical documents were examined alongside the knowledge of hereditary chiefs and elders. They explicitly acknowledge limits concerning narratives, territorial detail, and language. Their work offers an important sustained reading path without making one study a complete or timeless statement of Lake Babine law.

Read the sources [1] Lake Babine Nation Treaty Office [3] Jo-Anne Fiske and Betty Patrick · UBC Press

03

Trade, salmon, and historical records

The treaty office reproduces Daniel Williams Harmon’s account of his January 1812 journey among Babine villages. It describes hospitality, salmon-based livelihoods, and trade connections reaching toward the coast through neighboring peoples. The office also warns that Harmon’s knowledge was limited by observation and interpretation. His writing is a record of a colonial visitor encountering an already connected society. It does not mark the beginning of Babine history, establish an exact population, or supply an objective description of every community. Reading the excerpt with the office’s commentary makes the source’s position visible.

Read the sources [4] Lake Babine Nation Treaty Office

04

The barricade dispute and community resistance

In its account of 1906, the treaty office describes women defending a rebuilt fishing weir when fisheries officers attempted to dismantle it. It recounts arrests and negotiations in which chiefs sought provisions and services in exchange for removal of the weirs. The account calls the resulting agreement the Barricade Treaty. This history connects colonial control of fishing to food security, resistance, and political negotiation. A later UNBC report describes archaeological work conducted with Lake Babine Nation at a Babine River fishing village, where earlier work had established occupation extending back at least 1,300 years. The collaborative study concerns a particular site, not a date for the origins of the people.

Read the sources [5] Lake Babine Nation Treaty Office [6] University of Northern British Columbia

05

Language learning and public resources

Nedut’en is the name used by Lake Babine Nation’s FirstVoices collection. Its public pages offer an alphabet, recordings, words, phrases, and stories; individual records identify contributors. These are community-created learning resources, with their own access and reuse conditions. FPCC’s March 2025 account adds a specific example of intergenerational learning: Brian Lacerte learning from his mother, Rosalie MacDonald, through a mentor-apprentice program. It also describes MacDonald’s own learning and teaching work. Together, the collection and dated account show different forms of language transmission. Neither provides grounds for a current speaker census or a claim that one teaching method represents every family.

Read the sources [7] Lake Babine Nation · FirstVoices [8] First Peoples’ Cultural Council, with Odette Auger

06

Planning, governance, and the Foundation Agreement

The 2017–2022 community plan records priorities in language, education, housing, access, health, and stewardship, developed through engagement with members. It is evidence of community priorities during a stated planning period; it is not a report that all goals were achieved. The Nation’s November 2020 update explains the Foundation Agreement as a twenty-year framework for implementing rights and developing self-government, rather than a finalized treaty settlement. Its governance page describes a proposed Nation-level and community-level model and steps toward ratification and implementation. A February 2024 federal announcement records a further funding agreement supporting governance capacity and infrastructure priorities for Wit’at and Tachet. That announcement documents commitments, not the completion of all funded facilities or a transition to the proposed government.

Read the sources [2] Lake Babine Nation [9] Lake Babine Nation [10] Lake Babine Nation [13] Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada

07

Stewardship and decisions about development

Lake Babine Nation’s environmental-assessment explanation identifies sustainability, benefits, socioeconomic effects, and respectful relationships as criteria for evaluating proposed development. It distinguishes an assessment collaboration agreement from work toward a further consent agreement. A different publication, issued in July 2023, announced closure of the recreational salmon fishery along part of the Babine River corridor in response to warm water and pressure on salmon. Read as a dated action, it shows how stewardship is expressed through decisions concerning food, water, and future generations. The notice should not be used as current fishing guidance. More recent regulations and Nation communications would need checking before a visit.

Read the sources [11] Lake Babine Nation [12] Lake Babine Nation

What needs further research

  • Read the full Fiske–Patrick volume and subsequent community scholarship; compare accounts of women’s leadership, law, colonial violence, relocation, and residential schooling.
  • Follow the Barricade Treaty account into the original instrument, archival correspondence, and community interpretations of unfulfilled obligations. Compare the community plan’s 1905 chronology with the treaty office’s 1906 narrative.
  • Add more histories authored by individual communities and clarify the wider scope of historical Babine and related language labels.
  • Check newer community reports for the outcomes of governance, infrastructure, environmental-assessment, and language initiatives. Source quantity does not establish completion.
